newsitem.title: BURUNDI: U.N. fears for 100,000 missing Burundi refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. fears for 100,000 missing Burundi refugees.

text.p: The United Nations said on Sunday it feared for 100,000 Burundian Hutu refugees missing, without access to food or water, since they fled camps in eastern Zaire last month.

Burundi's Hutu refugees -- eclipsed by more than a million Rwandan Hutus -- have been forgotten by the outside world despite having no U.N. protection for three weeks, a United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) envoy said.

"There are more than 100,000 Burundi refugees missing and they have no food or water. If there is no food there is a risk of starvation. If there is no drinkable water there is a risk of epidemic," UNHCR Burundi representative Hitoshi Mise said.
"The international community talks about the Rwandan refugees around Goma, but they forget to talk about the refugees stuck in the Bukavu and Uvira region," Mise said.
Regardless of who is talked about more, no aid has reached the refugees from either nation, who are cut off by fighting.
The Hutus fled refugee camps around Goma, Bukavu and Uvira in eastern Zaire when fighting erupted between the Zairean army and local Tutsi rebels who now control much of eastern Zaire.
Uvira was the first town to fall to the rebels and the Hutu refugees from Burundi's civil war have been missing for three weeks, longer than those further north near Goma.

Around 140,000 of the 230,000 refugees who fled the Uvira camps were Burundian Hutus. About 40,000 have been accounted for, many of them having been forced to go home. Some 90,000 Rwandan Hutus who fled the Uvira camps are also missing.

Zaire's border with Burundi is now sealed and aid workers say they can only guess that some Burundi refugees have fled south towards Fizi, on the western shore of Lake Tanganyika, while others have gone west into inhospitable mountains.
Thousands of people have fled from the Fizi area across the lake into Tanzania, but most of them so far are displaced Zaireans -- the third group uprooted by regional conflict.
U.N. plans for military intervention to provide humanitarian assistance for the refugees are stalled.
"They will all be dead by the time the U.N. makes up its mind what to do," a senior U.N. official in Burundi warned.

Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya said on Saturday he welcomed military intervention to aid refugees stranded in Zaire, but that he opposed the use of military force to resolve Burundi's political problems.

Meanwhile, aid agency Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF, Doctors Without Borders) criticised UNHCR's policy of sending thousands of Burundian Hutus, who have returned home since the fall of the Uvira camps, to the troubled Cibitoke region in the northwest.
Insecurity in Cibitoke left the United Nations with limited access to the returnees, many of whom were sent to places lacking clean water or food, MSF said in a statement.
"MSF is particularly indignant about the repatriation of Burundians to their communes of origin, not least because UNHCR has no access to the area for security reasons," it said.
The United Nations plans to run a convoy with water, food, medicine and other supplies to the Cibitoke returnees on Tuesday.
Buyoya has denied reports by aid workers and diplomats that up to 140 Hutus returning home from the camps in Zaire were massacred by his army in an operation to identify Hutu rebels.
Around 150,000 people -- mainly civilians -- have died in Burundi in three years of fighting since the country's first elected Hutu president was murdered in an attempted coup.
Regional African states imposed economic sanctions on Burundi on July 31, six days after a military coup ousted Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya and brought Buyoya to power.
